name: Evaluating Psychological Criteria
what: This subtopic focuses on the strengths and limitations of each of the five psychological criteria used to categorise behaviour as typical or atypical. Understanding both sides of each criterion allows for more accurate and fair assessments of behaviour.
why: No single criterion provides a complete picture. Each has contexts in which it works well and contexts in which it fails or misleads. Knowing these limitations prevents over-reliance on any one measure and supports more nuanced clinical judgement.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of cultural perspectives as a criterion
items.what: Cultural perspectives are useful because they allow different cultural contexts to be taken into account and support collective evaluation of behaviour. The limitation is that in multicultural societies, multiple cultural norms intersect, making it difficult to isolate which cultural influences are relevant.
items.why: A criterion that ignores culture risks pathologising normal cultural practices. However, in diverse societies, it becomes harder to determine which cultural framework should apply to a given individual, reducing the criterion's precision.
items.example: A psychologist working with a client from a culture where emotional restraint is valued might correctly recognise that not expressing distress openly is culturally typical. But in a multicultural city where the client has lived across multiple cultural contexts, it may be unclear which cultural norm best applies to their behaviour.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of social norms as a criterion
items.what: Social norms are useful because they provide a clear baseline for comparison, making atypical behaviour relatively easy to identify. The limitation is that social norms are context-dependent, so the same behaviour may be typical in one setting and atypical in another, requiring additional effort to assess accurately.
items.why: Baselines simplify identification of divergence. But a criterion that shifts depending on context demands more interpretive work and risks producing inconsistent conclusions if context is not carefully considered.
items.example: Cheering loudly is typical at a football game but atypical during a formal debate. A psychologist assessing someone who cheers during a debate must account for context before concluding the behaviour is atypical, rather than simply applying a general social norm.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of statistical rarity as a criterion
items.what: Statistical rarity is useful because it provides an objective, measurable way to categorise behaviour that reduces subjective bias. The limitations are that not all statistical rarities indicate harm or dysfunction, and it can be difficult to apply percentages to abstract or variable human behaviours.
items.why: Objectivity is valuable in psychological assessment, but objectivity alone does not determine whether a behaviour is problematic. A statistically rare behaviour may be highly positive, neutral, or harmful, and numbers cannot always capture the nuance of individual behaviour.
items.example: Scoring in the top 0.1% on a mathematics test is a statistical rarity, but it is not a sign of atypicality in any concerning sense. Conversely, attempting to quantify what percentage of people feel a certain emotion on a given day is difficult because emotional expressions vary enormously between individuals.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of personal distress as a criterion
items.what: Personal distress is useful when cultural, statistical, and social criteria are not applicable, and it can provide visible evidence that a person is behaving differently from their norm. The limitation is that many individuals conceal or suppress distress, making it hard for others to detect and therefore hard to use as a reliable indicator.
items.why: Distress is a meaningful signal of change, but it relies on some degree of observable or reportable evidence. When individuals mask their distress, the criterion becomes unreliable and may result in underidentification of atypical behaviour.
items.example: A person who is usually calm and talkative suddenly becomes quiet and tearful in social situations. The visible distress makes it straightforward to identify atypical behaviour. However, a different person experiencing the same internal state but choosing to appear composed would be harder to identify using this criterion alone.

items.title: I can evaluate the usefulness and limitations of maladaptive behaviour as a criterion
items.what: Maladaptive behaviour is useful because it focuses on the consequences of behaviour, allowing the assessor to consider whether what appears problematic is actually harmful to functioning. The limitation is that judgements about what counts as maladaptive are subjective and can vary depending on who is making the assessment.
items.why: Focusing on functional consequences grounds assessment in real-world impact rather than appearance alone. However, subjectivity in defining 'effective functioning' means two assessors could reach different conclusions about the same behaviour.
items.example: One person might see a student avoiding conversation before an exam as maladaptive avoidance, while another might see it as a useful calming strategy. The same behaviour receives opposite categorisations depending on the assessor's interpretation of what counts as adaptive coping.
